#### From interval probabilities to a density

*Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Probability Density Functions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/random-variables.html#probability-density-functions),
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
Selected English explanation; notation and equation layout adapted.*

For a short interval of width $\epsilon$ near a point where the density
is continuous,

$$
P(X\in[x,x+\epsilon])
\approx \epsilon\,p(x).
$$

First, probabilities are never negative, thus we should expect that
$p(x)\ge0$ as well.

Second, let's imagine that we slice up $\mathbb R$ into an infinite number
of slices which are $\epsilon$ wide, say with slices
$(\epsilon i,\epsilon(i+1)]$. For each slice, the probability is
approximately $\epsilon p(\epsilon i)$, so summed over all of them
it should be

$$
P(X\in\mathbb R)
\approx\sum_i\epsilon\,p(\epsilon i).
$$

This is an approximation of an integral. Since the random variable must
take on some value, the total probability is one:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(x)\,dx=1.
$$

Over a finite interval, the same construction gives

$$
P(a<X\le b)=\int_a^b p(x)\,dx.
$$

![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/probability-native-2026-10-30/d2l-density-interval.svg]]

*The filled region under the density curve represents an interval
probability, not the height of the curve at a point. D2L shades the
sampled curve from $x=-2$ to $x=2.99$; its grid sum with step $0.01$
approximates $P(-2\le X<3)$ by about $0.7736$.
Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Probability Density Functions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/random-variables.html#probability-density-functions).
Complete original course SVG, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).*

Непрерывная величина равномерно распределена между $0{,}9$ и $1{,}6$.

Ширина этого интервала равна $1{,}6-0{,}9=0{,}7$. Поэтому высота плотности

#### Cumulative distribution function

The cumulative distribution function records the probability of being
at or below a threshold:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x).
$$

For a variable with density $p$, this is

$$
F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p(u)\,du.
$$

It is non-decreasing: increasing the threshold cannot remove any outcomes
from the event. Its limits at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$ are zero and one.
For the uniform example above,

$$
F(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0.9,\\
\dfrac{x-0.9}{0.7},&0.9\le x\le1.6,\\
1,&x>1.6.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus $P(1.0<X\le1.2)=F(1.2)-F(1.0)=2/7$, the same area calculated
above. For a discrete variable, $F$ has a jump at each outcome with
positive mass; the size of the jump equals that outcome's probability.
The definition $F(x)=P(X\le x)$ applies to both cases.

*Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Cumulative Distribution Functions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/random-variables.html#cumulative-distribution-functions),
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/);
the uniform worked example is expanded here.*

#### Marginalization for a joint density

*Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Joint Density Functions and Marginal Distributions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/random-variables.html#joint-density-functions),
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
Selected English explanation; equations split for narrow screens.*

For two continuous random variables, a small square has probability
approximately

$$
\begin{aligned}
&P(x<X\le x+\epsilon,\ y<Y\le y+\epsilon)\\
&\qquad\approx\epsilon^2p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\end{aligned}
$$

The joint density is non-negative and integrates to one over the plane.
To find the distribution of $X$ alone, we include every possible value
of $Y$.

Recall that the density is the function $p_X$ so that

$$
P(X\in[x,x+\epsilon])
\approx\epsilon\,p_X(x).
$$

There is no mention of $Y$, but if all we are given is $p_{X,Y}$,
we need to include $Y$ somehow. We can first observe that this is the same as

$$
\begin{aligned}
&P(X\in[x,x+\epsilon],\ Y\in\mathbb R)\\
&\qquad\approx\epsilon\,p_X(x).
\end{aligned}
$$

We split the $Y$-axis into intervals of width $\epsilon$ and add their
probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon\,p_X(x)
&\approx\sum_i\epsilon^2p_{X,Y}(x,\epsilon i).
\end{aligned}
$$

![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/probability-native-2026-10-30/d2l-marginal.svg]]

*By summing along the columns of our array of probabilities, we are able
to obtain the marginal distribution for just the random variable
represented along the $x$-axis. Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Fig. 22.6.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/random-variables.html#fig-marginal).
Complete original SVG, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).*

After canceling one factor of $\epsilon$, the sum becomes an integral
over $y$ in the limit:

$$
p_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy.
$$

This tells us that to get a marginal distribution, we integrate over
the variables we do not care about. This process is often referred to as
*integrating out* the unneeded variables.

For example, take the joint density $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=4xy$ on the unit square
$0\le x,y\le1$, and zero outside it. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_X(x)&=\int_0^1 4xy\,dy\\
&=4x\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^1=2x,
\qquad 0\le x\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting density is normalized: $\int_0^1 2x\,dx=1$.
Consequently, $P(X\le1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}2x\,dx=1/4$.
This extends the earlier column sum: sums eliminate discrete variables,
and integrals eliminate variables represented by densities.

### Maximum likelihood for continuous variables

*Aston Zhang et al.,
[D2L, Maximum Likelihood for Continuous Variables](https://d2l.ai/chapter_appendix-mathematics-for-deep-learning/maximum-likelihood.html#maximum-likelihood-for-continuous-variables),
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
English explanation adapted; the finite-window qualification and the
worked solution of Exercise 1 are expanded here.*

Everything that we have done so far assumes we are working with discrete
random variables, but what if we want to work with continuous ones?

We replace probabilities at observed values with densities and optimize

$$
-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_\theta(x_i).
$$

The question becomes, "Why is this OK?" After all, the reason we
introduced densities was because probabilities of getting specific
outcomes themselves were zero.

Suppose that, instead of requiring an exact measurement, we record
whether each observation falls in a small interval of width $\epsilon$.
The width is fixed independently of $\theta$. For $N$ independent
observations, define

$$
E_\epsilon
=\bigcap_{i=1}^{N}\{X_i\in[x_i,x_i+\epsilon]\}.
$$

Assume that each density is continuous and positive at the observed
value. For small $\epsilon$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_\theta(E_\epsilon)
&=\prod_{i=1}^{N}
\int_{x_i}^{x_i+\epsilon}p_\theta(u)\,du\\
&\approx\epsilon^N\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_\theta(x_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking negative logarithms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\log P_\theta(E_\epsilon)
&\approx-N\log\epsilon\\
&\quad-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_\theta(x_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first term does not depend on $\theta$, so it does not affect the
optimization of this small-interval approximation. The density is not
a probability of an exact observation; it describes how interval
probabilities scale with the measurement width.

For a fixed, non-negligible measurement interval, use its integrated
probability. Its maximizing parameter need not be exactly the same as
the density's maximizing parameter.

#### One observation from an exponential distribution

D2L's first exercise gives the density

$$
p_\alpha(x)=
\begin{cases}
\alpha e^{-\alpha x},&x\ge0,\\
0,&x<0,
\end{cases}
\qquad \alpha>0,
$$

and one observation, $x=3$. The likelihood and its negative logarithm are

$$
\mathcal L(\alpha)=\alpha e^{-3\alpha},
\qquad
-\log\mathcal L(\alpha)=3\alpha-\log\alpha.
$$

Differentiating gives $3-1/\alpha=0$, so $\hat\alpha=1/3$.
The second derivative is $1/\alpha^2>0$ on $\alpha>0$; this is the
unique minimum of NLL.

If the recorded event is instead $3\le X\le4$, its probability is

$$
P_\alpha(3\le X\le4)
=e^{-3\alpha}(1-e^{-\alpha}).
$$

Its log-derivative is $-3+1/(e^\alpha-1)$, whose zero occurs at
$\hat\alpha=\log(4/3)\approx0.28768$, rather than $1/3$.
For a general width $\epsilon$, the maximizer is

$$
\hat\alpha_\epsilon
=\frac{\log(1+\epsilon/3)}{\epsilon}
\longrightarrow\frac13
\quad\text{as }\epsilon\to0.
$$

source_caveats: D2L maximum-likelihood.md line 221 omits a minus sign on the right-hand side of the NLL derivative; this equation is not copied. The chapter derives the correct signs independently.

D2L's finite-epsilon wording is qualified: dropping the width term applies to the small-interval approximation, not an exact optimizer equality for arbitrary measurement widths. The exponential worked example demonstrates the difference.
D2L's numerical log example uses a base-10 value. The chapter explicitly uses natural logarithms and retains its independently checked 2000-factor example.
